summary.text: The liver is a major metabolic organ found only in vertebrates, located in the right upper abdomen below the diaphragm.
It detoxifies the body, makes proteins and other biochemicals needed for digestion and growth, and converts and stores nutrients such as glucose and glycogen.
As an accessory digestive organ it produces bile, which emulsifies and aids the break up of dietary fat.

facts.label: Size rank
facts.value: Heaviest internal organ and largest gland

facts.label: Functional units
facts.value: Hepatic lobules, each of millions of hepatocytes

facts.label: Blood supply
facts.value: The hepatic artery and the portal vein

items.prompt: Someone calls the liver the body's chemical factory. What is the reasoning?

options.label: It makes all the body's red blood cells
It carries out around 500 different functions
It is the only organ that makes bile and saliva
It is the body's largest muscle

items.explain: Its tissue regulates a wide variety of biochemical reactions, with around 500 functions generally cited.

items.prompt: After a fatty meal, which substance helps break the fat into smaller droplets, and where is it made?

options.label: Amylase, made by the salivary glands
Mucin, made by the lining of the mouth

items.explain: The liver produces bile, an alkaline fluid that emulsifies and aids the break up of dietary fat.

items.prompt: Blood carrying freshly digested nutrients from the intestines arrives at the liver through which vessel?
items.explain: The portal vein carries blood rich in digested nutrients from the gastrointestinal tract; the hepatic artery brings oxygen-rich blood from the aorta.

items.prompt: As of 2018, what was the only option for complete liver failure?
items.explain: Dialysis works only in the short term, artificial livers have not been developed for long-term use, and transplantation was the only option.

items.prompt: Where is bile kept and concentrated until it is needed in digestion?
items.explain: The gallbladder sits just under the right lobe of the liver and stores and concentrates the bile the liver produces.

items.prompt: A person takes a knock to the lower right ribs. Why is the liver mostly protected there?

options.label: It sits in the left upper abdomen behind the lower left ribs
It sits in the right upper abdomen, shielded by the lower right rib cage
It sits in the pelvis behind the hip bone
It sits in the chest above the diaphragm

items.explain: In humans the liver lies in the right upper abdomen below the diaphragm and is mostly shielded by the lower right rib cage.

paragraphs.heading: The body's chemical factory
paragraphs.text: The liver is a major metabolic organ, and only vertebrates have one. It clears toxins from the body and makes many proteins and other substances needed for digestion and growth. It also handles carbohydrates, makes several hormones, converts and stores nutrients such as glucose and glycogen, and breaks down red blood cells. Counts of its jobs differ, but around 500 is the usual figure, which is why it is sometimes called the body's chemical factory. Medical words about the liver often use the prefix hepat-, from the Greek word for it, as in hepatitis.

paragraphs.heading: Where it sits and how big it is
paragraphs.text: In people the liver sits in the upper right part of the abdomen, just below the diaphragm, mostly sheltered by the lower right ribs. It is dark reddish brown and wedge-shaped. A human liver usually weighs about 1.5 kilograms and is about 15 centimetres wide, though sizes vary a lot between people: the normal range is 970 to 1,860 grams for men and 600 to 1,770 grams for women. No other internal organ in the human body weighs more, and no gland is bigger. Across vertebrates, too, it is the largest internal organ.

paragraphs.heading: Making bile
paragraphs.text: The liver also helps digestion by making bile, an alkaline fluid holding cholesterol and bile acids. Bile emulsifies dietary fat, helping to break it up. The gallbladder, a small hollow pouch just under the liver's right lobe, stores the bile and concentrates it, then later sends it into the duodenum to help digest food.

paragraphs.heading: Blood in, work done
paragraphs.text: Two large blood vessels supply the liver. The hepatic artery brings oxygen-rich blood from the aorta, while the portal vein brings blood full of digested nutrients from the whole gastrointestinal tract, along with blood from the spleen and pancreas. These vessels branch into tiny capillaries called liver sinusoids, which lead into hepatic lobules, the working units of the liver. Each lobule holds millions of hepatocytes, the basic cells of metabolism, which carry out a huge range of reactions that build and break down molecules.

paragraphs.heading: Lobes and landmarks
paragraphs.text: Seen from above, the liver has two parts, a right and a left lobe, split on the surface by the falciform ligament, a fold of the thin membrane that covers it. Seen from below there are four lobes: left, right, caudate and quadrate, with the two extra ones lying between the main pair, one in front of the other. An imagined line running from the left of the vena cava forward splits the liver and gallbladder into two halves. It is called Cantlie's line.

paragraphs.heading: No lasting substitute
paragraphs.text: There is still no lasting stand-in for a working liver. Liver dialysis can cover for it over a short time, but no one knows how to make up for missing liver function in the long term, and artificial livers have not been developed for long-term replacement. As of 2018, a transplant is the only option when the liver fails completely.
